title: Dream Machine: Scaling to 1m users in 4 days — Keegan McCallum, Luma AI
talk_summary: Luma AI's infra lead recounts scaling Dream Machine from 500 to ~9,000 H100s in days, replacing brittle Triton serving with a decoupled PyTorch-based pull-queue architecture, and fixing work starvation with SLO-percentage-based fair scheduling. The transferable core is queue/scheduling design and immutable versioned model rollouts, not GPU specifics.

takeaways.technique: SLO-percentage fair scheduling for work queues
takeaways.what_they_do: Instead of naive priority order (which starves low tiers) or raw aging, they rank queued jobs by the percentage of their tier's SLO already consumed, so a 1-min-waiting API job competes equally with a 10-min-waiting free job.
takeaways.evidence_quote: we ranked the jobs by the percentage of their SLO um that they that they were at
takeaways.numbers: free-tier users previously waited 7-9 hours under naive priority

takeaways.technique: Decoupled pull-based workers over shared queue + storage
takeaways.what_they_do: CPU workers and GPU workers are decoupled; any worker anywhere connects to Redis and distributed storage (SeaweedFS) over Tailscale and pulls from a global queue, so new capacity needs no special provisioning.
takeaways.evidence_quote: you can actually run the GPUs anywhere as long as you can connect to Reddus and our distributed storage
takeaways.numbers: scaled 500 -> ~5,000 H100s in 6 hours, later ~9,000 total

takeaways.technique: Dispatch limitation / back-pressure cap per cluster
takeaways.what_they_do: They cap how many jobs can sit in the 'pulled but not yet picked up by a worker' state per cluster, so one cluster's CPU workers don't hoard jobs that another cluster could process.
takeaways.evidence_quote: you can put a limitation on like how many jobs are in that state so that you can avoid this this issue

takeaways.technique: Immutable versioned model/env repo with YAML active pointer
takeaways.what_they_do: Each model is a folder in object storage with immutable versioned subfolders containing checkpoints and the full Python environment; a root YAML names the active version, and workers hot-swap versions without restarting.
takeaways.evidence_quote: you have a simple YAML file in the root of the model folder that lets you define which one's active

takeaways.technique: Avoid wasteful cold-start autoscaling for heavy models
takeaways.what_they_do: Because models are 10-20 submodels with long compile/warmup, traditional autoscaling wastes 10-20 min of GPU time per cold start; they keep warm pools and scale on the training cluster instead.
takeaways.evidence_quote: traditional autoscaling is super wasteful. You're wasting, you know, 10 20 minutes of GPU time just warming things up

takeaways.technique: Product-defined SLOs as the aging function
takeaways.what_they_do: Rather than engineers guessing an aging curve, the product team defines worst-case acceptable wait per tier, and that config drives scheduling thresholds (e.g., promote at 50% of SLO).
takeaways.evidence_quote: this is a product problem and it really comes down to how long worst case are you okay with different tiers waiting
